sections.title: Troubleshoot Mobile OS and Application Security Issues
sections.file: 3.3 Troubleshoot Mobile OS and Application Security Issues.html

terms.name: Blue screen of death (BSOD)
terms.definition: Windows stops with a blue screen when bad hardware, bad drivers, or a failing app prevents the OS from continuing. Note the stop code / QR details for targeting the right fix.
terms.scenario: After a new GPU driver, the PC dies on a solid blue stop screen with a QR code and hex dump. What crash is that?

terms.name: Last Known Good Configuration
terms.definition: Boot into the last successful startup registry and driver set after a bad driver or config change.
terms.scenario: A driver change wrecked boot. You want the last successful startup registry and driver set — not a restore point. What feature is that?

terms.name: System Restore
terms.definition: Roll system files, drivers, and settings back to a restore point without wiping personal documents.
terms.scenario: You need to roll Windows files, drivers, and settings back to a snapshot without wiping Documents. What tool do you use?

terms.name: Roll back drivers
terms.definition: In Device Manager, undo a recently installed driver that started the crashes.
terms.scenario: Crashes started right after yesterday’s display driver. In Device Manager you undo just that driver. What is that action called?

terms.name: Safe Mode
terms.definition: Boot with only essential drivers/services so you can remove bad software or roll back drivers that block a normal start.
terms.scenario: Windows will not start normally. You boot with only essential drivers so you can uninstall the bad software. What boot mode is that?

terms.name: Reseat components
terms.definition: Power down and reseat RAM, GPU, and power connectors — loose hardware often looks like a software stop error.
terms.scenario: Stop codes look like software, but RAM and the GPU were never clicked fully home. What hardware step do you try first?

terms.name: Hardware diagnostics
terms.definition: Run UEFI/BIOS or vendor tools to test CPU and RAM when stop codes point at memory or kernel faults.
terms.scenario: The stop code points at memory or the kernel. You run UEFI/vendor tests on CPU and RAM. What kind of check is that?

terms.name: Boot issues
terms.definition: Windows fails to start normally — missing OS/bootloader, dual-boot conflicts, or the system only reaches Safe Mode. Non-bootable media can also block startup.
terms.scenario: The machine never reaches a normal desktop — missing bootloader, dual-boot fight, or it only lands in Safe Mode. What class of problem is that?

terms.name: Remove non-bootable media
terms.definition: Unplug USB installers, external drives, and optical discs that the firmware may try to boot before the OS disk.
terms.scenario: Firmware keeps trying a leftover USB installer before the Windows disk. What do you pull first?

terms.name: Startup Repair
terms.definition: Use the automated WinRE tool first when Windows fails to start or only boots into Safe Mode.
terms.scenario: Windows fails to start or only reaches Safe Mode. You try WinRE’s automated fix before any command-line tools. What is that tool?

terms.name: bootrec /rebuildbcd
terms.definition: From the Recovery Console, rebuild the Boot Configuration Database when Startup Repair is not enough.
terms.scenario: WinRE’s automated fix did not restore boot. From Recovery Console you rebuild the Boot Configuration Database. Which command?

terms.name: “No OS found”
terms.definition: The firmware or bootloader cannot find a bootable OS — often bootloader corruption, dual-boot overwrites, or missing boot files.
terms.scenario: Firmware or the bootloader cannot find any bootable operating system. What message/condition is that?

terms.name: Unplug non-bootable drives
terms.definition: Disconnect extra media and secondary disks so firmware boots the correct Windows volume.
terms.scenario: An extra HDD and an optical drive are in the boot order, so firmware never hits the real Windows volume. What do you disconnect?

terms.name: Startup Repair
terms.definition: Let WinRE repair missing or damaged boot files that trigger a “No OS found” message.
terms.scenario: The PC reports no operating system. You let WinRE repair missing or damaged boot files before typing commands. What tool is that?

terms.name: bootrec /rebuildbcd
terms.definition: Manually rebuild the BCD from the Recovery Console command prompt if Startup Repair does not restore boot.
terms.scenario: “No OS found” is still there after WinRE. From the recovery command prompt you rebuild the BCD by hand. Which command?

terms.name: Degraded performance
terms.definition: The PC feels slow or unresponsive — apps lag, disk thrashing is high, or tasks take longer than normal.
terms.scenario: Apps lag, the disk thrashes, and everyday tasks take longer than they used to. What symptom is that?

terms.name: Task Manager
terms.definition: Use Processes and a ~60-second Performance view to find the apps consuming CPU, disk, or memory.
terms.scenario: You open Processes and watch Performance for about a minute to see which app is eating CPU, disk, or RAM. What utility is that?

terms.name: Windows Update checks
terms.definition: Install pending OS patches that fix known performance bugs and resource leaks.
terms.scenario: Pending OS patches are known to fix the resource leak causing the slowness. What check do you run?

terms.name: Free disk space
terms.definition: Clear unused files so the volume has headroom for paging, updates, and temp files.
terms.scenario: The volume is packed, so paging, updates, and temp files have nowhere to go. What do you free up?

terms.name: Defrag (HDD)
terms.definition: On hard disks, run Optimize/Defragment. Skip routine defrag on SSDs — they use TRIM/optimize instead.
terms.scenario: The PC uses a spinning hard disk, not an SSD. You run Optimize/Defragment. What maintenance is that?

terms.name: Laptop power source
terms.definition: Seat the charger firmly — on battery or a weak adapter, Windows may throttle the CPU.
terms.scenario: A laptop is slow until you click the charger in firmly — Windows was throttling on battery. What did you check?

terms.name: Antivirus scan
terms.definition: Run a full scan when Task Manager shows unexplained high CPU or disk use from malware.
terms.scenario: Task Manager shows unexplained high CPU and disk with no heavy app open. You run a full scan for malware. What scan is that?

terms.name: Low memory warnings
terms.definition: Windows warns that memory is nearly full — apps may freeze, crash, or refuse to open while RAM pressure is high.
terms.scenario: Windows pops a banner that RAM is nearly full; apps freeze or refuse to open. What warning is that?

terms.name: Close memory-heavy apps
terms.definition: Sort Task Manager by Memory, save work, then close or restart the programs using the most RAM.
terms.scenario: You sort Task Manager by Memory, save work, and quit the browsers eating most of the RAM. What step is that?

terms.name: Virtual memory (paging file)
terms.definition: Review the paging file under System > About > Advanced system settings > Performance Settings > Virtual Memory.
terms.scenario: You open Advanced system settings → Performance → Virtual Memory to review the paging file. What setting is that?

terms.name: Frequent shutdowns
terms.definition: The system powers off or stops without a scheduled shutdown — often hardware faults, corrupted system files, or malware.
terms.scenario: The PC powers off with no shutdown click — not a scheduled restart. What symptom is that?

terms.name: Full hardware diagnostics
terms.definition: Test motherboard, CPU, and RAM with UEFI/BIOS or vendor diagnostic tools.
terms.scenario: Unexpected power-offs continue. You run UEFI/vendor tests on the motherboard, CPU, and RAM. What kind of test is that?

terms.name: Windows Memory Diagnostics
terms.definition: Reboot into the built-in RAM test when random power-offs suggest memory errors.
terms.scenario: Random power-offs smell like bad RAM. You reboot into Windows’ built-in memory test. What tool is that?

terms.name: System File Checker (sfc)
terms.definition: Run sfc /scannow to repair corrupted Windows files that can force unexpected stops.
terms.scenario: Unexpected stops look like damaged Windows files. You run sfc /scannow. What tool is that?

terms.name: Anti-malware scan
terms.definition: Scan for malware that can crash services or force the machine offline.
terms.scenario: The machine keeps dropping offline and killing services; you scan for malware that can force those stops. What scan is that?

terms.name: System instability
terms.definition: Random crashes, freezes, or reboots with no single app clearly to blame.
terms.scenario: Random crashes, freezes, and reboots with no single app to blame. What symptom is that?

terms.name: Full hardware diagnostics
terms.definition: Stress-test CPU, RAM, and related hardware when there is no clear software cause.
terms.scenario: Instability has no software lead. You stress-test CPU, RAM, and related hardware. What kind of test is that?

terms.name: Windows Memory Diagnostics
terms.definition: Run the built-in RAM test when freezes or BSODs look memory-related.
terms.scenario: Freezes and blue screens look memory-related. You run the built-in RAM test. What tool is that?

terms.name: System File Checker (sfc)
terms.definition: Scan and repair corrupted Windows system files with sfc /scannow.
terms.scenario: Random instability continues. You scan and repair corrupted Windows system files. What tool is that?

terms.name: Anti-malware scan
terms.definition: Scan for malware that injects into processes or tampers with system files.
terms.scenario: Processes look injected and system files keep changing. You scan for malware tampering with the OS. What scan is that?

terms.name: Time drift
terms.definition: The clock slowly loses accuracy because of unreliable hardware timekeeping — which can break auth, certificates, and sync.
terms.scenario: The clock slowly loses minutes, and Kerberos tickets plus HTTPS certs start failing. What problem is that?

terms.name: Set time automatically
terms.definition: In Settings > Time & Language > Date & Time, enable automatic time (and DST) so Windows syncs to time servers, or sync manually.
terms.scenario: In Date & Time you turn on automatic time (and DST) so Windows syncs to time servers. What setting is that?

terms.name: Services not starting
terms.definition: Windows or third-party services fail to start, leaving features offline until drivers, permissions, or dependencies are fixed.
terms.scenario: Print Spooler and a backup agent never come up after reboot, so those features stay offline. What symptom is that?

terms.name: Device Manager
terms.definition: Check device status, then update, roll back, or replace drivers that block related services.
terms.scenario: A yellow bang on a device is blocking the related service. You update, roll back, or replace the driver there. What console is that?

terms.name: services.msc
terms.definition: Start the service manually, adjust the log-on account, and verify dependencies in the Services app.
terms.scenario: You open the Services app, start the service, fix the log-on account, and check dependencies. What MMC is that?

terms.name: sfc /scannow
terms.definition: Repair corrupted built-in Windows service binaries. For third-party app services, reinstall the app with admin rights.
terms.scenario: A built-in Windows service will not start because its binary is corrupt. You repair system files; for a third-party service you would reinstall the app. Which command?

terms.name: Applications crashing
terms.definition: One or more programs close unexpectedly, hang, or fail to stay open during normal use.
terms.scenario: One program keeps closing, hanging, or refusing to stay open during normal use. What symptom is that?

terms.name: Event Viewer / Reliability Monitor
terms.definition: Inspect crash logs and reliability history to identify the failing module or recent change.
terms.scenario: You check crash logs and reliability history to see which module or recent change killed the app. What pair of tools is that?

terms.name: Reinstall the application
terms.definition: Repair or reinstall the failing app after logs point to a corrupted install.
terms.scenario: Logs say the install is corrupted, so you repair or put the same program back on the PC. What step is that?

terms.name: USB controller resource warnings
terms.definition: Connecting a device exceeds the USB controller’s available endpoints, so Windows warns or the device misbehaves.
terms.scenario: Plugging in a webcam triggers a warning that the USB controller is out of endpoints. What warning is that?

terms.name: Move to another USB port
terms.definition: Disconnect the device and plug it into a different port or controller to free endpoints.
terms.scenario: The USB device misbehaves on this port, so you unplug it and try a different port or controller. What step is that?

terms.name: Balance USB 2.0 / 3.0
terms.definition: Keep USB 2.0 devices on USB 2.0 controllers and USB 3.0 devices on USB 3.0 controllers to spread endpoint load.
terms.scenario: You keep USB 2.0 gadgets on 2.0 controllers and USB 3.0 gadgets on 3.0 so endpoints are not stacked on one hub. What practice is that?

terms.name: Slow profile load
terms.definition: Sign-in takes a long time, usually from network latency or WAN congestion while syncing a roaming profile to a domain controller.
terms.scenario: Domain sign-in takes forever while a roaming profile crawls over a congested WAN to the DC. What symptom is that?

terms.name: Repair / optimize domain controllers
terms.definition: Domain admins fix or optimize local DCs and profile sync paths so roaming profiles load without WAN bottlenecks.
terms.scenario: Help desk escalates to domain admins to fix local DCs and profile sync so logon is not waiting on the WAN. What fix is that?

terms.sectionTitle: Troubleshoot Mobile OS and Application Issues
terms.name: Application fails to launch
terms.definition: Restart the device. Update the app. Reinstall the app.
terms.scenario: A phone app will not open at all. After a reboot you update it, then reinstall it. What issue are you working?

terms.sectionTitle: Troubleshoot Mobile OS and Application Issues
terms.name: Application fails to close / crashes
terms.definition: Force close the app. Restart the device. Update the app. Reinstall the app. Review crash logs / contact support.
terms.scenario: The app is stuck on screen or dies mid-use. You force-close it, reboot, update, then reinstall and check crash logs. What issue is that?

terms.sectionTitle: Troubleshoot Mobile OS and Application Issues
terms.name: Application fails to update
terms.definition: Update the app. Check payment method. Check network / try another network. Check storage space. Restart the device. Check MDM policy.
terms.scenario: The store will not patch the app. You check payment, network, storage, reboot, and MDM before trying again. What issue is that?

terms.sectionTitle: Troubleshoot Mobile OS and Application Issues
terms.name: Application fails to install
terms.definition: Check storage space. Check payment method. Check network / try another network. Check MDM policy.
terms.scenario: A new app will not install. Storage, payment method, network, and MDM policy are the first checks. What issue is that?

terms.sectionTitle: Troubleshoot Mobile OS and Application Issues
terms.name: Slow to respond
terms.definition: Restart the device. Update the app. Update the OS.
terms.scenario: The phone feels laggy in one app. You reboot, then update the app and the OS. What symptom is that?

terms.sectionTitle: Troubleshoot Mobile OS and Application Issues
terms.name: OS fails to update
terms.definition: Check storage space. Check network / try another network. Restart the device.
terms.scenario: The phone OS update will not finish. You free storage, try another network, and reboot. What issue is that?

terms.sectionTitle: Troubleshoot Mobile OS and Application Issues
terms.name: Battery life issues
terms.definition: Airplane Mode (poor coverage). Turn off unused radios (Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, GPS). Check battery health. Replace the battery.
terms.scenario: The phone dies by lunch. You try Airplane Mode in poor coverage, kill unused radios, then check battery health. What issue is that?

terms.sectionTitle: Troubleshoot Mobile OS and Application Issues
terms.name: Random reboots
terms.definition: Update the OS. Update the app. Review crash logs / contact support. Check battery health.
terms.scenario: The phone restarts by itself. You update OS and apps, review crash logs, and check the battery. What symptom is that?

terms.sectionTitle: Troubleshoot Mobile OS and Application Issues
terms.name: Connectivity issues — Wi-Fi
terms.definition: Toggle the radio off and on (Wi-Fi / Bluetooth / NFC). Verify Wi-Fi password / AP settings. Check network / try another network. Restart the device.
terms.scenario: The phone will not join the office SSID. You toggle Wi-Fi, recheck the password/AP, try another network, then reboot. What issue is that?

terms.sectionTitle: Troubleshoot Mobile OS and Application Issues
terms.name: Connectivity issues — Bluetooth
terms.definition: Toggle the radio off and on (Wi-Fi / Bluetooth / NFC). Restart the device. AirDrop: Bluetooth + Wi-Fi on; move closer.
terms.scenario: Headphones will not pair. You toggle Bluetooth, reboot, and for AirDrop you also turn Wi-Fi on and move closer. What issue is that?

terms.sectionTitle: Troubleshoot Mobile OS and Application Issues
terms.name: Connectivity issues — Near-field communication (NFC)
terms.definition: Toggle the radio off and on (Wi-Fi / Bluetooth / NFC). Restart the device. Update linked payment cards.
terms.scenario: Tap-to-pay will not fire. You toggle NFC, reboot, and update the cards in the wallet app. What issue is that?

terms.sectionTitle: Troubleshoot Mobile OS and Application Issues
terms.name: Screen does not autorotate
terms.definition: Check orientation lock. Close and reopen the app. Restart the device. Hardware failure — contact support.
terms.scenario: Turning the phone sideways does not rotate the screen. You check orientation lock, reopen the app, then reboot. What issue is that?

terms.sectionTitle: Troubleshoot Mobile OS and Application Security Issues
terms.name: Application source / unofficial application stores
terms.definition: Sideloading apps from third-party sites or APK files poses severe security risks because uncurated sources may contain malware that can access device data.
terms.scenario: The user sideloaded an APK from a random website instead of the official store. What risk source is that?

terms.sectionTitle: Troubleshoot Mobile OS and Application Security Issues
terms.name: Developer mode
terms.definition: Enables advanced OS access, USB debugging, memory statistics, and detailed logging capabilities.
terms.scenario: USB debugging, verbose logs, and extra OS switches are turned on for tinkering. What mode is that?

terms.sectionTitle: Troubleshoot Mobile OS and Application Security Issues
terms.name: Root access / jailbreak
terms.definition: Modifies core firmware to override the factory operating system, granting complete control over the device and enabling sideloading.
terms.scenario: The user patched firmware to override the factory OS so they can sideload anything and own the device. What modification is that?

terms.sectionTitle: Troubleshoot Mobile OS and Application Security Issues
terms.name: Unauthorized / malicious application
terms.definition: Unapproved apps or infected development environments (e.g., XcodeGhost) can inject malicious code, harvest data, or secretly sign users up for paid services without consent.
terms.scenario: An unapproved app — or a poisoned Xcode-style toolchain — is harvesting data and signing the user up for paid services. What kind of app is that?

terms.sectionTitle: Troubleshoot Mobile OS and Application Security Issues
terms.name: Application spoofing
terms.definition: Malicious apps masquerade as legitimate tools (e.g., photo editors or QR scanners) while performing hidden malicious actions in the background.
terms.scenario: A “photo editor” icon is a fake; the real work is hidden in the background. What technique is that?

terms.sectionTitle: Troubleshoot Mobile OS and Application Security Issues
terms.name: High network traffic
terms.definition: Unexpected spikes in data transmission can indicate a malware infection, such as command-and-control communications or encrypted traffic proxying.
terms.scenario: Cellular graphs spike at night with no streaming. You suspect C2 or proxy traffic. What symptom is that?

terms.sectionTitle: Troubleshoot Mobile OS and Application Security Issues
terms.name: Degraded response time
terms.definition: Unresponsive screens, sluggish app performance, or choppy animations can be caused by resource-heavy malware or buggy software.
terms.scenario: The screen feels sticky, apps hitch, and animations stutter — malware or a buggy app is chewing resources. What symptom is that?

terms.sectionTitle: Troubleshoot Mobile OS and Application Security Issues
terms.name: Data-usage limit notification
terms.definition: Reaching a cellular data threshold — using native Android limits/warnings or third-party monitoring apps — can serve as an early warning sign that background malware is exfiltrating data.
terms.scenario: The carrier warning says the monthly cellular cap is already hit, which can be an early sign of data leaving the phone. What notification is that?

terms.sectionTitle: Troubleshoot Mobile OS and Application Security Issues
terms.name: Limited internet connectivity
terms.definition: Malware or misconfigurations can degrade network performance.
terms.scenario: Wi-Fi and cell still show bars, but pages crawl because malware or a bad config is degrading the path. What symptom is that?

terms.sectionTitle: Troubleshoot Mobile OS and Application Security Issues
terms.name: No internet connectivity
terms.definition: Malware may intentionally block internet connections to prevent anti-malware definition updates or security software downloads.
terms.scenario: The phone has no usable internet at all — malware may be blocking it so security tools cannot update. What symptom is that?

terms.sectionTitle: Troubleshoot Mobile OS and Application Security Issues
terms.name: High number of ads
terms.definition: Persistent or excessive ad pop-ups are often driven by adware or fake ad-blocking malware (e.g., Fake Ads Block) designed to generate ad revenue for attackers.
terms.scenario: Pop-up ads cover every screen, often from adware or a fake “ad blocker.” What symptom is that?

terms.sectionTitle: Troubleshoot Mobile OS and Application Security Issues
terms.name: Fake security warnings
terms.definition: Malicious browser pop-ups imitate official system alerts to trick users into downloading “security updates” that actually install malware.
terms.scenario: A browser overlay pretends to be an OS alert and begs the user to “update security,” which would install malware. What symptom is that?

terms.sectionTitle: Troubleshoot Mobile OS and Application Security Issues
terms.name: Unexpected application behavior
terms.definition: Sudden crashes, unresponsiveness, broken features, or excessive battery drain are typically app-specific bugs.
terms.scenario: One app suddenly crashes, drains battery, and loses features while the rest of the phone is fine. What symptom is that?

terms.sectionTitle: Troubleshoot Mobile OS and Application Security Issues
terms.name: Leaked personal files / data
terms.definition: Caused by local malware breaches or compromised cloud storage accounts.
terms.scenario: Photos and contacts showed up on a forum; likely local malware or a hijacked cloud account. What incident is that?

terms.name: Unable to access the network
terms.definition: Malware can intentionally block network access to prevent downloading anti-malware tools or installing operating system security patches that close known vulnerabilities.
terms.scenario: The Windows PC cannot reach the network at all — malware may be blocking patches and AV downloads. What symptom is that?

terms.name: Desktop alerts
terms.definition: Rogue browser pop-ups or pushed web messages often impersonate official system notifications to trick users into extending fake subscriptions or downloading malicious software.
terms.scenario: Rogue browser messages impersonate Windows notifications and push a fake subscription. What symptom is that?

terms.name: False alerts regarding antivirus protection
terms.definition: Scareware mimics legitimate security tools, claiming your system is disabled or infected with specific threats (e.g., Trojan spyware). They direct users to call fake tech support numbers or pay money.
terms.scenario: A scareware window claims Defender is disabled and a Trojan is active, then shows a fake support number. What symptom is that?

terms.name: Altered system or personal files
terms.definition: Files or system binaries are unexpectedly renamed, moved, or missing.
terms.scenario: Documents and system binaries were renamed, moved, or are just gone. What symptom is that?

terms.name: Unwanted notifications within the OS
terms.definition: Operating systems allow apps to push unwanted pop-ups.
terms.scenario: Installed apps keep pushing pop-ups through the OS notification center. What symptom is that?

terms.name: OS update failures
terms.definition: Malware, network misconfigurations, firewall filtering rules, or network bandwidth caps can block system updates.
terms.scenario: Windows Update will not finish — malware, a firewall rule, or a bandwidth cap may be blocking it. What symptom is that?

terms.name: Random / frequent pop-ups
terms.definition: Fake application prompts appear despite modern browser pop-up blockers being enabled by default.
terms.scenario: Fake app prompts keep appearing even though the browser’s pop-up blocker is on. What symptom is that?

terms.name: Certificate warnings
terms.definition: Browsers display “connection is not private” or untrusted site errors. Click the lock icon next to the HTTPS URL to inspect certificate details.
terms.scenario: The browser says the connection is not private. You click the lock next to HTTPS to inspect the cert. What warning is that?

terms.name: Redirection
terms.definition: Entering a search query or URL redirects the user to unintended, illegitimate websites designed to display ads or distribute further malware.
terms.scenario: Typing a normal search or URL dumps the user on a junk ad or malware site. What browser issue is that?

terms.name: Degraded browser performance
terms.definition: Sluggish loading and high system resource usage can be caused by excessive open tabs, bloated browser caches, or malicious JavaScript (e.g., background crypto miners using 100% CPU).
terms.scenario: The browser is sluggish and CPU sits at 100% — too many tabs, a bloated cache, or a JS miner. What symptom is that?
